lines.text: This one lake beats all five Great Lakes.
How does it beat all five, if it's barely bigger than Belgium?
Meet Lake Baikal, in Siberia. The Great Lakes are not impressed.
We're almost eight times bigger!
lines.speaker: superior

lines.text: On a map? Sure. So where is Baikal hiding all that water?
Straight down.
Baikal plunges 1,642 metres. About four times deeper than Lake Superior.
Nobody asked you to measure.
lines.speaker: superior

lines.text: That's nearly five Eiffel Towers deep.
But why so deep? Baikal isn't sitting in a valley. It's filling a crack in the Earth.
Right here, the ground is slowly pulling apart.
That crack opened 25 to 30 million years ago. Which makes Baikal the oldest lake on Earth.
The Great Lakes? They filled up about 14,000 years ago.
Can we change the topic?
lines.speaker: superior

lines.text: And the crack is still opening. About four millimetres, every year.
Width makes a lake look big. Depth makes it big.
Here's the twist. The water isn't even the bottom.
Below the lake floor lies up to seven kilometres of mud. The crack goes down about as far as Everest is tall.
chunks: LIES UP TO|*SEVEN KILOMETRES* OF MUD.
ABOUT AS FAR AS|*EVEREST* IS TALL.

lines.text: And from above? It still looks barely bigger than Belgium.
Why do I keep getting dragged into this?
lines.speaker: belgium
